historical-universe.html.title: Who disappears from a historical panel?
historical-universe.html.normalizedText: Methods note · Protocol proposal A historical panel can look complete after its least visible members have disappeared. A defensible analysis needs to say who was eligible at each date, who exited, and what each exit means for the outcome. Status: source-cited protocol proposal, not an empirical finding. This note does not analyze ODGS companies, select its issuer universe, or claim a project data source is available. Selection and exit are part of the data A panel assembled only from entities still present today can exclude entities whose disappearance is related to the outcome. The mechanism and direction depend on the unit, endpoint, and exit process. “Survivorship bias” is a reason to examine selection; it is not a universal correction factor. For stock-return data, Shumway documented missing delisting returns for many stocks delisted for negative reasons and found the omitted returns were large in the setting studied. Dropping terminal returns in that setting can make measured return histories too favorable. That result does not imply a fixed adjustment for other samples or outcomes. [1] For mutual funds, Elton, Gruber, and Blake followed funds that existed at the end of 1976 and accounted for merger terms when funds merged. Their design shows why disappeared entities and exit treatment belong in the research record. [2] CRSP’s current product description lists active and inactive securities, permanent identifiers, corporate actions, and delisting information. These fields may support historical-universe research, but a product description does not establish project access, complete coverage for a particular question, or a valid reconstruction. [3] Proposed audit Define the target population and observation unit at each historical date. Record eligibility and entry using information available then. Preserve stable entity and security identifiers through name changes, reorganizations, mergers, and share-class changes. A ticker or current company name is not a permanent identity. Retain entities that exit the observable universe. Record exit date, exit type, source, and whether the entity was delisted, bankrupt, merged, acquired, liquidated, renamed, or became unobserved. Predefine what the estimand means after each exit. For returns, account for terminal returns, distributions, and merger consideration when available. For other outcomes, distinguish a true zero, competing event, censoring, and missing follow-up. Report panel coverage and exit counts by date and exit type. Compare included and excluded entities using information known before the endpoint. Run sensitivity analyses for unresolved exit values or coverage gaps. State which conclusions depend on those choices. Limits The cited studies concern particular financial datasets and questions. This note does not estimate a bias for ODGS or set its population, outcome, or source. The project remains at specification and source-feasibility stage; access to CRSP or another historical return source has not been confirmed. The checklist is a proposed research-control protocol, not a tested result. Takeaway A historical panel needs an explicit account of who enters, who exits, and how exits affect observation and outcome measurement. Keep population selection, terminal outcomes, censoring, and source missingness distinct so readers can see which assumptions affect each result. Sources Shumway T. “The Delisting Bias in CRSP Data.” The Journal of Finance . 1997;52(1):327–340. doi:10.1111/j.1540-6261.1997.tb03818.x . Elton EJ, Gruber MJ, Blake CR. “Survivorship Bias and Mutual Fund Performance.” The Review of Financial Studies . 1996;9(4):1097–1120. doi:10.1093/rfs.9.4.1097 . Center for Research in Security Prices. CRSP US Stock Databases . Product description; access and project-specific coverage remain unverified. Prepared for the independent scientific notes collection · September 2026

nmr-thermodynamic-inference.html.title: When NMR peak height supports a thermodynamic inference
nmr-thermodynamic-inference.html.normalizedText: Research note · Coauthored study A temperature-dependent spectral signal becomes a thermodynamic claim through a model. The strength of that claim depends on the controls and independent measurements that test the same interpretation. Scope: evidence-chain analysis of one published study. The study is coauthored. Its paper identifies Nicholas J. Sisco and Minjoo Kim as equal contributors, and credits N.J.S. with experiments, data analysis, and manuscript writing. This note does not claim sole authorship. From resonance intensity to a state transition In a study of the isolated human TRPV1 S1–S4 membrane domain, Kim and colleagues followed assigned NMR resonances across temperature. They report reversible, sigmoidal peak-height changes for resonances that could be assigned and tracked, then fit a two-state thermodynamic model to estimate residue-level enthalpy behavior. [1] The paper also reports simulations for an idealized rigid protein under similar conditions. Those simulated peak-height profiles were not sigmoidal. This control supports the conformational-transition interpretation, while leaving the measurement and model assumptions open to inspection. How the inference was checked Peak height is an observed spectral quantity; a thermodynamic transition is an interpretation of how that quantity changes with temperature. The study strengthened that interpretation with several additional measurements. Far-UV circular dichroism and intrinsic fluorescence showed similar temperature-dependent behavior. Other NMR experiments probed distance, secondary structure, and solvent exposure. Whole-cell patch-clamp measurements and a coupling-disrupting mutation connected the isolated-domain observations to channel activation. This structure of evidence matters because resonance loss, emergence, overlap, exchange behavior, and acquisition conditions can complicate the mapping from signal to mechanism. A useful analysis makes the steps visible: Define which peaks are assigned and traceable across the temperature series; record excluded or ambiguous peaks. State the fitted model and its assumptions, and retain fit diagnostics rather than reporting only a derived parameter. Compare the observed pattern with an explicit control or simulation that could produce a different pattern. Seek orthogonal evidence with different sensitivities. Here the study combines NMR peak behavior with CD, fluorescence, structural NMR, and electrophysiology. Keep conclusions at the scale tested. Isolated-domain behavior informs a proposed mechanism; linking it to full-channel function requires separate evidence. Limits This note summarizes one coauthored study and does not independently reanalyze its data. The interpretation is specific to the TRPV1 constructs, conditions, and models in that paper. Temperature-dependent peak-height fitting is not a general replacement for structural or functional validation, and an isolated domain does not reproduce every interaction in a full-length channel. Takeaway The strongest inference did not come from treating a changing NMR peak as a direct measurement of thermodynamics. It came from making the measurement model explicit, checking a competing signal explanation, and connecting the result to orthogonal structural and functional evidence. Source Kim M, Sisco NJ, Hilton JK, et al. “Evidence that the TRPV1 S1-S4 membrane domain contributes to thermosensing.” Nature Communications . 2020;11:4169. DOI · Open full text . The article is open access under CC BY 4.0 . No figure or article text is reproduced here. Prepared for the independent scientific notes collection · September 2026

problem-of-evil.html.title: A child dies: proximity, explanation, and the problem of evil
problem-of-evil.html.normalizedText: Philosophy · Philosophy of religion The same suffering can feel like an abstraction at a distance and unbearable when it is near. That change in our attention does not settle what the suffering means. It does sharpen the question posed to a God who, by definition, would know every case. The question. How should we understand intense suffering in a world governed by a God traditionally described as all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good? This note distinguishes a logical challenge from an evidential one, tests several familiar explanations, and asks what human proximity adds to the discussion. Two versions of the problem The logical problem claims that the existence of evil is incompatible with the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God. A strict contradiction requires more than the observation that these ideas sit uneasily together: it needs premises showing that a good God would prevent every evil that an all-powerful God could prevent. One influential reply is Alvin Plantinga’s free-will defense. Its task is limited but important: to describe a possible reason God might permit some moral evil, such as preserving significant creaturely freedom. If that account succeeds as a defense of possibility, the bare claim of formal contradiction is weakened. It does not show that human freedom explains the suffering we actually observe, or that every instance of suffering is justified. [1] The evidential problem asks a different question: given the amount, intensity, distribution, and apparent pointlessness of suffering, how likely is a perfectly good and powerful God? William Rowe’s example of a fawn suffering unseen in a forest fire presses on this question. The fawn’s pain is not an obvious result of anyone’s wrongdoing, and no human witness seems needed for the event to occur. The argument is not that we have proved no reason could exist; it is that some suffering appears to have no morally sufficient reason, and that appearance bears on the evidence. [2] Who or what is doing the harming? It helps to separate moral evil , which arises from choices such as cruelty or violence, from natural suffering , which arises through disease, earthquakes, congenital conditions, predation, and other natural processes. Free will may address some cases of human wrongdoing. By itself, it does not explain childhood illness, an animal’s slow death, or suffering that predates human beings. Appeals to Satan or to a primordial Fall can supply a story about how evil entered creation. But in classical monotheism Satan is still a created being; the Fall is still part of a world God creates or permits. These accounts can identify a proximate cause without resolving the question of ultimate permission: why would an omnipotent God allow that cause to produce this scope and duration of suffering? That is better described as explanatory displacement than as begging the question. Begging the question, in its strict sense, assumes the conclusion an argument is supposed to establish. Naming Satan does not necessarily do that. It may instead move the explanatory burden to God’s decision to create, sustain, or not prevent Satan’s actions. Likewise, the Fall may explain suffering within a theological framework while leaving open whether the proposed consequences are proportionate or fit the natural history we observe. What might suffering be for? Theodicies offer possible goods that might explain why God permits suffering. A free-will account connects some moral evil to meaningful agency. A soul-making account treats hardship as a setting for courage, compassion, or moral growth. Other replies appeal to stable natural laws, goods that depend on those laws, an afterlife in which wrongs are repaired, or limits on what humans can know about divine reasons. Each proposal has a scope and a cost. Freedom may explain why people can harm one another, but it is less direct for earthquakes or animal pain. Growth may follow from some hardship, but severe suffering can destroy a person’s capacities rather than develop them. Stable laws make an intelligible world possible, but the question remains why they must permit these particular harms. Future restoration could matter morally, yet compensation does not automatically explain why the suffering had to happen. Skepticism about our ability to see God’s reasons cautions against overconfidence; taken too far, it can also make claims about divine goodness difficult to assess. The evidential challenge therefore does not require the claim that no suffering could have a reason. It asks whether the range of explanations gives adequate reason to expect a world with this much apparently unnecessary suffering, including cases where no clear good seems to be served. Belief, story, and self-persuasion Explanations do more than answer questions. They can also preserve commitments people already depend on. When “God is good,” “God is in control,” and “this suffering is real” collide, people may add an account involving freedom, a Fall, a hidden plan, or eventual compensation. A community can refine and reinforce such accounts over generations without any single person designing the whole system. This is a reason to examine explanations carefully, not a proof that religious belief is false or that believers are uniquely gullible. The same human habit appears wherever people protect an important worldview: we seek coherence, notice confirming examples, and learn familiar answers from people we trust. A useful check is to ask what evidence could count against a proposed explanation, whether it addresses this kind of suffering, and whether it is being used as a possibility or as an established fact. Proximity changes the weight we feel An unknown child dying painfully may pass through our minds as one fact among millions—or never enter our awareness. Give the child a name, a face, a family, and a place beside us, and the same event can become morally immediate. The event has not changed; our access to it has. Physical distance is only one kind. A relationship, photograph, detailed account, or resemblance to someone we know can make a distant person feel close. Research on responses to identifiable and statistical victims finds that vivid, individually presented cases can draw different emotional and giving responses than aggregate descriptions. That tells us something about human attention; it does not show that one life matters more than many, or decide whether God exists. [3] For a human observer, concern is partial and often rises with proximity. For an omniscient God, however, there would be no informational distance: no anonymous child, unseen animal, or forgotten instance. This makes the familiar reassurance “there must be a reason” harder to treat as a simple appeal to cases we cannot picture. The question returns in concrete form: Why was this suffering necessary? Then it returns across every life that has suffered. What the argument leaves open The problem of evil is not one isolated syllogism with one uncontested conclusion. The logical version asks whether the claims can coexist; the evidential version weighs what the world’s suffering suggests. The free-will defense can answer one kind of logical objection without settling the evidential question. Satan and the Fall can form parts of a theology without ending the question of divine permission. Proximity reveals how our own moral attention works, but it does not alter the underlying facts or prove a metaphysical conclusion on its own. The hardest question is cumulative: whether any account of freedom, growth, natural order, hidden reasons, or eventual repair makes the actual history of suffering intelligible—and whether that account is independently persuasive, rather than merely a way to keep the starting commitments intact. Further reading Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “ The Logical Problem of Evil ,” including discussion of Plantinga’s free-will defense. William L. Rowe, “ The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism ,” American Philosophical Quarterly 16, no. 4 (1979): 335–341. Deborah A. Small, George Loewenstein, and Paul Slovic, “ Sympathy and Callousness: The Impact of Deliberative Thought on Donations to Identifiable and Statistical Victims ,” Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 102, no. 2 (2007): 143–153. This is a philosophical essay, not a claim that a theological or atheistic conclusion has been proven. The psychological research describes human responses; it is not evidence about divine knowledge.

the-moment-is-over.html.title: The Moment Is Over
the-moment-is-over.html.normalizedText: Experimental writing · Short story A morning coffee ritual wanders through memory, measurement, color, existential thought, and the uncomplicated love of an old dog. Writing experiment. This piece explores how detail and thought can accumulate around an ordinary routine, moving between recollection, inner argument, sensory observation, and affection. I love my coffee routine. I walk into my pantry and think about how this whole setup came together. It always goes the same way in my mind. I remember the extreme amounts of coffee I used to consume during undergrad and grad school. Then, one day, I stopped. I was sick at the time, and the withdrawal humbled me. Then I remember how much I liked the efficiency of espresso. So I experimented, and one day I got lucky: someone gifted me a small, cheap espresso machine. I love it. The coffee comes in compostable, biodegradable packaging, sealed immediately after grinding. I figure it’s about as good an espresso as I, or even a well-trained person, could make—within 90% confidence intervals. And I am perfectly fine living in that space now. See, I have grown. I wander over to the coffee machine, barely awake. I notice my house around me. What a blessing this is. I watch my beautiful Cavalier King Charles spaniel eat his food. He is eleven years old, a perfect, purebred Blenheim. As I turn on the machine, I sniff the coffee before delicately placing the packets to make a double espresso. I know it sounds like a lot. I think about this as well. I’m a little obsessed with this. I explain to my inner interlocutors that no, in fact, two espressos—especially prepared this way, by me, an amateur at best—have less caffeine than a twelve-ounce cup of drip coffee. At least, that’s the case I make. You see, it’s all about concentration… And my inner interlocutor gives up. My cup is ready. My dog is ready to go outside. I open my side door and am greeted by the most beautiful backyard beneath a delicate, brand-new sky, just peeking through, testing to see whether the sun wants to come out. The soft, deep blue mixed with those delicate but piercing yellows and oranges is a feast for the eyes. Our bodies evolved to see these colors, and somehow we also find them beautiful. Then there are the mathematical relationships across the electromagnetic spectrum, color theory, complementary colors, all of it. Human color vision is a gift that is hard to explain. I ponder qualia and existential philosophy, imagining myself discussing how we should live when the universe is monstrously indifferent to the plight of man. That phrase is meant to shock the interlocutor, you see. The point is to get you to see the void. Once you see it, you must face it. Jeez, this coffee is hot. Good hot. The kind of hot where I’m a little proud of how much that hurt. Then my dog catches my eye, smiles at me, and darts off like he’s been waiting for me to look at him this whole time before doing his business. I love that dog so much it’s hard to describe. That taste of coffee. I was about to wax philosophical about existential philosophy. If my interlocutors groaned during the concentration conversation earlier, they’ve left the room now. Once Nick gets on existential philosophy, it’s over. The party is over. The thing I’ve grown to like most about this espresso… is how fast the moment is over. Then my dog wants in, so we come back inside, and my house greets me. This is my dream.
